hook.text: Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books for years. The fraud was hiding in plain sight.

buildup.text: Andersen earned $25 million in audit fees and $27 million in consulting fees from Enron annually.

discovery.text: The consulting revenue created a conflict: challenge the client and risk losing a $52 million account.

twist.text: Andersen partners overruled internal concerns about Enron's accounting to keep the client happy.

climax.text: When the scandal broke, Andersen's reputation was destroyed faster than any audit could have saved.

punchline.text: The auditor chose the fees over the truth.

quiz.question: What conflict of interest did Arthur Andersen face with Enron?
options: Earning more from consulting than auditing the same client
Having former Enron employees on staff

details.summary: The Enron scandal and Arthur Andersen's role in it is the most consequential audit failure in history. Andersen's destruction of documents and conflicts of interest led to its collapse and triggered sweeping reforms in the audit profession.
details.whyItMatters: The Enron scandal fundamentally reshaped auditing regulation, created the PCAOB, passed Sarbanes-Oxley, and demonstrated what happens when audit independence is compromised — making it the most studied case in audit history.
takeaways: Arthur Andersen earned more in consulting fees from Enron than audit fees, creating a massive conflict of interest
Andersen's destruction of audit documents during the SEC investigation was the final blow to the firm
The scandal led directly to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and creation of the PCAOB oversight board

faq.question: What did Arthur Andersen do wrong in the Enron audit?
faq.answer: Andersen failed to challenge Enron's aggressive accounting, partly because it earned enormous consulting fees from Enron and didn't want to lose the client. When the SEC began investigating, Andersen employees shredded thousands of audit documents. The firm was convicted of obstruction of justice.

faq.question: How did the Enron scandal change auditing?
faq.answer: It led to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, which created the PCAOB to oversee public company auditors, banned audit firms from providing certain consulting services to audit clients, required CEO/CFO certification of financial statements, and dramatically increased penalties for financial fraud.
